newsitem.title: USA: Strong dollar may have widened U.S. trade deficit.
newsitem.headline: Strong dollar may have widened U.S. trade deficit.

text.p: The White House said on Monday that the main factor contributing to the worsening in the U.S. trade deficit was weak growth abroad, but said it was possible that the dollar's strength may have played a role.

"In 1996, slower growth in economic activity in our major foreign markets negatively affected U.S exports," the White House said in the annual Economic Report of the President prepared by the Council of Economic Advisers (CEA).

"Although weak growth in our trading partners was the main cause of the increased deficit, the strength of the dollar against the yen and the major continental European currencies may also have played a small role," it added.

The report said the appreciation of the dollar in 1996 after having hit its lowest level in almost three years in mid-1995 helped explain part of the slowing in imports in late 1995 and the increase of imports in 1996.

U.S. manufacturers, particularly the major car companies, have complained that the rising dollar is taking a toll on their sales by making their products more expensive in global markets while making their competitors' products cheaper.

On Saturday, finance ministers from the Group of Seven rich industrialized nations signaled a desire to halt the dollar's rise. After meeting in Berlin, they said they wanted major currencies to stabilize around current levels.
But the White House report said the dollar's rise was probably not the dominant cause of recent increases in the U.S. trade deficit.

The report said that while the dollar has increased against some currencies, its effective exchange-rate index, when weighted according to trade shares, has appreciated only 6 percent in real terms since 1995.
The report predicted a pick up in U.S. exports in the coming year due to an expected increase in economic activity among key U.S. trading partners.

Joseph Stiglitz, chairman of the CEA, told reporters in an embargoed briefing last Friday that news that the German January unemployment rate had risen to 12.2 percent, compared with December's 10.8 percent, was a "cause for concern."
However, he said the diversification of the U.S. economy should help protect it from weakness in any one region.

"The news that came out today (on Friday) about the high level of unemployment in Germany is a cause for concern," Stiglitz said. "It Europe is weak, they are one of our main trading parters and they would demand less goods from us.
"The good thing about the American economy right now is it is a very diversified economy ... and so (whatever) happens in one particular market, we have a buffer with respect to other markets."
